blocks.prompt: 7. [Prove by mathematical induction:] \(1 + nx \le (1 + x)^n\) for \(n \ge 2\) and \(x > -1\).
blocks.explanation:
An inequality containing a letter \(x\), proved by extended induction on \(n\) starting at \(n = 2\) (this is Bernoulli's inequality).
The condition \(x > -1\) makes \(1 + x\) positive, so we may multiply by it safely.
Plan: base case by expanding \((1 + x)^2\); multiply the hypothesis by \(1 + x\); drop the term \(kx^2 \ge 0\).
steps:
Given: \(S(n): (1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx\), with \(x > -1\) fixed.
To prove: \(S(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge 2\).
Method: Extended mathematical induction on \(n\). From \(x > -1\): \(1 + x > 0\).

Base case: put \(n = 2\)
\[(1 + x)^2 = 1 + 2x + x^2\]
\[\ge 1 + 2x\]
So \(S(2)\) is true.
Why: \(x^2 \ge 0\) for every real \(x\); removing it can only make the right side smaller or equal.

Induction hypothesis: assume \(S(k)\), \(k \ge 2\)
\[(1 + x)^k \ge 1 + kx \quad (A)\]
Why: We suppose the inequality holds for some integer \(k \ge 2\).

Inductive step: multiply (A) by \(1 + x\)
\[(1 + x)^{k+1} = (1 + x)^k(1 + x)\]
\[\ge (1 + kx)(1 + x)\]
Why: \(1 + x > 0\), so multiplying both sides of (A) by it keeps the sign \(\ge\).

Expand and drop the extra term
\[(1 + kx)(1 + x) = 1 + x + kx + kx^2\]
\[= 1 + (k + 1)x + kx^2\]
\[\ge 1 + (k + 1)x\]
Why: \(k > 0\) and \(x^2 \ge 0\), so \(kx^2 \ge 0\); removing it gives "\(\ge\)".

Join the results
\[(1 + x)^{k+1} \ge 1 + (k + 1)x\]
So \(S(k + 1)\) is true.
Why: The two previous steps form one chain of \(\ge\) signs.

Conclusion
\(S(2)\) is true and \(S(k) \Rightarrow S(k + 1)\) for \(k \ge 2\). By the principle of extended mathematical induction, \(1 + nx \le (1 + x)^n\) for every integer \(n \ge 2\) and every \(x > -1\).
Why: Both conditions of the principle hold.

Check: \(n = 3,\ x = -\tfrac{1}{2}\)
\[(1 - \tfrac{1}{2})^3 = \tfrac{1}{8}\]
\[1 + 3(-\tfrac{1}{2}) = -\tfrac{1}{2} \le \tfrac{1}{8} \;\checkmark\]
Why: It holds even for a negative \(x\) (greater than \(-1\)).
blocks.final_answer: Hence proved: \(1 + nx \le (1 + x)^n\) for every integer \(n \ge 2\) and \(x > -1\).
